sections.h2: What the Medina County Recorder does
sections.html:
Land records for Medina County live permanently with the Recorder: deeds, mortgages, easements and any other paper that moves or burdens a piece of land. The office is at 144 N. Broadway Street, Room 117, in the city of Medina, and the main number is 330-725-9782. A document search page on the recorder's website lets you look up recorded deeds and mortgages from home.

Staff take in each paper, index it and keep it in archival form. They never rule on who owns a house. Your title company reads the index to confirm the chain of owners and to spot any open mortgage that has to be released at closing.

A deed costs $34 for its first two pages. Each extra page adds $8, and each marginal notation adds $4. Of every recording fee, half funds the recorder and half funds the Ohio Housing Trust Fund, as section 317.32 of the Ohio Revised Code requires.

Medina County Recorder fees

A county may tack on a preservation surcharge of up to five dollars. Before you mail a check, phone the office and ask for the exact total at your page count.

sections.h2: Who collects the transfer charge on a sale?
sections.html:
The county auditor collects it, and that happens before the deed reaches the recorder. On real property the conveyance fee runs $3.00 for every $1,000 of price, with the price rounded up to the next $100. The auditor's website has a calculator if you want a number before closing.

Ordinary sales use DTE Form 100. A transfer that qualifies for an exemption uses DTE Form 100EX. The auditor's exemption list covers:

  • gifts inside a family, such as spouse to spouse or parent to child;
  • property passing to an heir, a devisee or a surviving spouse;
  • a corrective or confirming deed for one already on record;
  • a court-ordered transfer that is not a sale;
  • a deed into a revocable trust.

Manufactured homes are charged $1.00 per $1,000 instead. Before the signing, ask the auditor which form your deed needs.

sections.h2: Which county offices a house sale touches
sections.html:
A house sale usually passes three counters in Medina, and the sequence matters. Reverse it and you lose a few days.

  • Auditor: takes the statement of value and the conveyance fee.
  • Recorder: records the endorsed deed, any mortgage release and any affidavit.
  • Treasurer: holds the real estate tax payoff. Your title company will want that payoff figure.

Professional filers can e-record and skip the trip. The office works with Simplifile, ePN and CSC eRecording Solutions, and File and Go covers notices of commencement. Each filer makes one ACH payment per day no matter how many documents go in, so nobody writes a check for the wrong amount.

Selling for cash changes nothing at these counters. There is no new mortgage to record, yet the auditor must still stamp the deed first.

sections.h2: Papers from a sale that go through the recorder
sections.html:
The recorder handles these documents at the standard rate. Most Medina County sellers will meet only a few of them.

  • Warranty, quit claim and survivorship deeds.
  • Sheriff's deeds, which close out a foreclosure sale.
  • Mortgages, mortgage releases, assignments and subordinations.
  • Affidavits, powers of attorney and various trust documents.
  • Land contracts, leases and easements.

An inherited house often needs an affidavit or certificate alongside the deed. A house with a lender needs a release recorded after payoff, which carries the $4 release fee. Each paper is priced separately by page count, so a closing with a deed, a release and an affidavit produces three charges.

sections.h2: Make your deed easy to record
sections.html:
A formatting law, ORC 317.114, has applied since July 1, 2009. A deed that falls short can be charged an extra $20. Get it right the first time and you skip both the charge and the call back.

Use a preparer who knows Ohio's format and legal description rules, and confirm the page total before you pay. Call 330-725-9782 with questions. The auditor's site also has a sales report of nearby parcels, handy for sanity-checking the price on your statement of value.

sections.h2: From signing to a recorded deed
sections.html:
On the records side, a typical sale runs in this order. If you know the sequence, you can see where a hold-up sits.

  • Your title company requests payoff figures from the treasurer and your lender.
  • You sign. The preparer completes the statement of value, DTE Form 100 for a normal sale or Form 100EX for an exempt one.
  • The auditor stamps the deed and takes the conveyance charge.
  • Next the stamped deed travels to the recorder, alongside a release if a lender is paid off.
  • Once indexed, the deed appears in the online search.

With a cash buyer, the lender steps drop out and the sale can move faster, since nobody waits on loan underwriting. The recording steps stay the same. Keep a copy of the recorded deed and the release for your own files after closing.

The county's population was 185,025 in July 2025. Eight in ten homes (80.3 percent) are lived in by their owners, across 73,086 households, so most recorded deeds here are ordinary owner-to-owner sales. Rental and inherited houses make up the rest.

  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $287,000.
  • Homeowners with a mortgage report $1,726 a month in costs; those without report $650.
  • Renters pay a median $1,143 in gross rent.
  • Household income reaches $94,968 at the median.
  • The county counted 77,727 housing units and issued 430 building permits during 2025.

The recorder offers a free Property Fraud Alert. Enroll on the recorder's website and an automated system emails or calls you whenever a transaction naming your property is recorded. That gives you a chance to catch a forged deed early. The office at 330-725-9782 can help with the sign-up.

A veteran can record a DD214 at no cost, and the office issues a free Veteran's Identification Card once the discharge is on file. Recording the paper creates a certified source if the original is ever lost.

faqs.q: Where is the Medina County Recorder's office?
faqs.a: It is at 144 N. Broadway Street, Room 117, Medina, Ohio 44256. The office phone is 330-725-9782. Call before you go to confirm hours and the total fee for your document.

faqs.q: What are the recording fees in Medina County?
faqs.a: The fee is $34 up to two pages and $8 per page beyond. A document that fails the state formatting rules draws an extra $20. Ask the office whether the optional preservation surcharge applies to your filing.

faqs.q: Does the recorder charge the real estate transfer tax?
faqs.a: No. The county auditor collects the conveyance fee, set at $3.00 per $1,000 of the sale price. Exempt transfers use DTE Form 100EX and pay no conveyance fee.

faqs.q: Can lenders and title agents e-record Medina County deeds?
faqs.a: Yes, through Simplifile, ePN or CSC eRecording Solutions, all under contract with the office. Homeowners generally do not e-record on their own, so ask your closing agent.

faqs.q: Can Medina County owners get an alert when a document hits their property record?
faqs.a: Yes. The recorder runs a free Property Fraud Alert program that sends an email or phone notice when a transaction involving your property is recorded.
